C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:236:Operating systems generally allow users to connect multiple screens to a single device and arrange them virtually to extend the overall visual workspace.
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:237:A variety of applications use platform tools to place their content in such multi-screen environments, but web application developers are limited by existing APIs, which were generally designed around the use of a single screen.
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:238:As multi-screen devices and applications become a more common and critical part of user experiences, it becomes more important to give web developers information and tools to leverage that expanded visual environment.

C:/tmp/spec_window.txt-251-Motivating Use Cases
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:252:The aim of this specification is enable better experiences for web application users with multiple screens. Here are some use cases that inform the design:
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:253:Slideshow app presents on a projector, shows speaker notes on a laptop screen.
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt-254-Financial app opens a dashboard of windows across multiple monitors.
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt-255-Medical app opens images (e.g. x-rays) on a high-resolution grayscale display.
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:256:Creativity app shows secondary windows (e.g. palette) on a separate screen.
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:257:Conference room app shows controls on a touch screen device and video on a TV.
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:258:Multi-screen layouts in gaming, signage, artistic, and other types of apps.
C:/tmp/spec_window.txt:259:Site optimizes content and layout when a window spans multiple screens.

name : Window Management
summary : Previously named "Multi-Screen Window Placement".

Adds new screen information APIs and makes incremental improvements to existing window placement APIs, allowing web applications to offer compelling multi-screen experiences.

The existing singular window.screen offers a limited view of available screen space, and window placement functions generally clamp bounds to the current screen. This feature unlocks modern multi-screen workspaces for web applications.

 motivation : As multi-screen devices and applications become a more common and critical part of user experiences, it becomes more important to give web developers information and tools to leverage that expanded visual environment. This feature incrementally extends the web platform's single-screen paradigm to support multi-screen devices.

Allowing script to query the device for information about its screens, and place content on specific screens enables many powerful multi-screen windowing behaviors. Use cases enabled by these APIs include:

- Slideshow app presents on a projector, shows speaker notes on a laptop screen.
- Financial app opens a dashboard of windows across multiple monitors.
- Medical app opens images (e.g. x-rays) on a high-resolution grayscale display.
- Creativity app shows secondary windows (e.g. palette) on a separate screen.
- Conference room app shows controls on a touch screen device and video on a TV.
- Multi-screen layouts in gaming, signage, artistic, and other types of apps.
- Site optimizes content and layout when a window spans multiple screens.

 activation_risks : This feature incrementally extends existing screen information and window placement interfaces with basic multi-screen support. This immediately enables new compelling experiences through progressive enhancement of existing applications.

 devtrial_instructions : https://github.com/w3c/window-management/blob/main/HOWTO.md

 comments : - First origin trial: Developer feedback (Google-internal doc) was generally straightforward: the API is useful, and it would be difficult or impossible to accomplish anything similar without it. The most common request was that it be made broadly available as soon as possible. There were two feature requests; and while neither is provided with this initial launch, the API shape does not preclude adding support:
to hide the location bar on popup windows
for getScreens() to return information about mirrored displays
- Feedback on Github: After the OT, @jakearchibald, @kenchris, and others gave feedback on the API shape <https://github.com/w3c/window-management/issues/30>. Changes were made accordingly <https://github.com/w3c/window-management/blob/main/CHANGES.md>.
- Second origin trial: Once again, developer feedback (Google-internal doc) was broadly positive. One feature was requested three times: the ability to open a new window and immediately make it fullscreen. This feature is on our roadmap. Demand for this API is high, and we want to give developers the chance to start using it as soon as possible. Thus it makes sense to launch an MVP, then add additional features like this one.

### 6218822004768768 Automatic Fullscreen Content Setting
summary : A new "Automatic Fullscreen" content setting permits Element.requestFullscreen() without a user gesture, and permits browser dialogs to appear without exiting fullscreen.

The setting is blocked by default. Sites can query for permission (starting in M128), but cannot prompt. New UI controls are limited to Chrome's settings pages [1] and the site info bubble. Users can allow Isolated Web Apps [2], and enterprise admins can allow additional origins with the AutomaticFullscreenAllowedForUrls policy.

Combined with Window Management permission [3] and unblocked popups [4], this unlocks valuable fullscreen capabilities:
- Open a fullscreen popup on another display, from one gesture
- Show fullscreen content on multiple displays from one gesture
- Show fullscreen content on a new display, when it's connected
- Swap fullscreen windows between displays with one gesture
- Show fullscreen content after user gesture expiry or consumption

[1] chrome://settings/content/automaticFullScreen and site details pages
[2] User control is initially scoped to security-sensitive apps; see https://chromestatus.com/feature/5146307550248960
[3] For multi-screen window placement features; see https://chromestatus.com/feature/5252960583942144
[4] To similarly permit window.open() without a user gesture; see chrome://settings/content/popups
all_platforms : False
all_platforms_descr : Initial support targets desktop platforms.

### 5173162437246976 Window Management: Fullscreen Companion Window
summary : Fullscreen Companion Window allows sites to place fullscreen content and a popup window on separate screens from a single user activation.

This is a small requested enhancement of the Window Management feature: https://chromestatus.com/feature/5252960583942144
all_platforms : False
all_platforms_descr : All Blink platforms have some support for multiple displays, but may restrict the placement and sizing of windows. The overall API will initially be exposed on desktop platforms, as developers have primarily voiced interest for use cases in desktop applications, and the added complexity of mobile and WebView support strongly exceeds developer enthusiasm for usage on those platforms.

C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:151:Installing and uninstalling PWAs
C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:152:While installing a PWA only takes a couple of clicks, depending on the web application features, the result of installing a PWA usually goes well beyond creating a link to a page on the Internet; installing a PWA more deeply integrates the web application on the user's device.

C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:154:Installing PWAs
C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:155:The UI for installing a PWA from the web varies from one browser to another, and from one platform to another.
C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:156:The user interface for installing PWAs differs by device and OS combination. The "Add to homes screen" user interface installs the PWA on Safari on iOS. C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:157:When the user selects the icon, the browser displays a prompt asking if they want to install the PWA, and if they accept, the PWA is installed.
C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:158:Once installed, the PWA will behave like other applications that are installed on the OS. For example, on macOS, the icon will appear in the dock, and will have the same icon options as other applications:
C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:159:On most desktop browsers, the install prompt is in the URL bar. On mobile, the install prompt is generally found in the menu of browser options. No matter the browser or OS, the installation needs to be confirmed.

It also means that you can install the same PWA from a different browser and that the two apps will behave as two different instances and will not share any data.
C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:172:The browser used to install the PWA will know the PWA is installed, but other browsers will not have access to the installed status. C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt:173:When you tap the web app's icon, it opens up in the browser environment that installed the PWA, generally without the browser's UI around it, though that depends on the way the developer configured the
C:/tmp/mdn_install.txt-174-web app manifest

I read this as a 2026 compatibility verification - I cross-checked compatibility datasets, vendor records, and specifications, then mapped each unsupported path to a concrete fallback.

# Browser and OS support as of 2026-08-13

## Bottom line

A deterministic experience that enumerates monitors, selects one, opens a window there, and makes it fullscreen remains a **desktop Chromium progressive enhancement**.

- **Chrome/Edge desktop:** full multi-screen path is available.
- **Firefox and Safari:** ordinary windows and fullscreen work, but there is no screen enumeration or scripted target-screen fullscreen.
- **Mobile and WebViews:** no Window Management API or target-screen fullscreen.
- **Presentation API:** Chromium-only and device/transport dependent. It presents through a browser-controlled chooser; it is not a substitute for deterministic monitor placement.
- **Installing a PWA does not make unsupported APIs available or remove popup, permission, or fullscreen restrictions.**
- No manifest member declaratively chooses a physical monitor or lays out several windows.

## Compatibility matrix

| Capability | Chrome desktop | Edge desktop | Firefox | Safari | Android Chromium | iOS/iPadOS | WebViews |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `getScreenDetails()` / `ScreenDetails` | 100+ | 100+ | No | No | No | No | No |
| `requestFullscreen({screen})` | 100+ | 100+ | No; option unsupported | No; option unsupported | No | No | No |
| Fullscreen plus companion popup from one activation | 104+ | Chromium equivalent | No | No | No | No | No |
| Ordinary `requestFullscreen()` | 71+ | 79+ | 64+ | 16.4+ | Yes | iPad partial; not iPhone | Android WebView yes; iOS WebView no |
| Presentation API | 47+ | 79+ | No | No | Yes in Chrome-family browsers | No | No |
| `launch_handler` | 110+ | 110+ | No | No | Implemented, but platform normally routes to one app client | No | Not a useful installed-app surface |
| Multiple installed PWA windows | Yes on desktop | Yes on desktop | No native desktop PWA installation | Safari web apps exist, but no launch-handler placement control | Generally single-client | Generally single-client | N/A |

Desktop Chrome support covers **Windows, macOS, Linux, and ChromeOS**. Chrome Status explicitly records Window Management as desktop-only; Android, WebView, and iOS milestones are absent. Edge inherits the Chromium implementation on its supported desktop systems.

Other Chromium desktop browsers are marked as mirrored implementations in MDN browser-compat-data, but product behavior and policy can differ. Feature detection is preferable to naming Opera, Brave, or another Chromium product as guaranteed.

## 1. Window Management API

### Supported behavior

On desktop Chromium, after the `window-management` permission is granted:

- `screen.isExtended` reports whether an extended display arrangement is exposed.
- `getScreenDetails()` returns individual `ScreenDetailed` objects.
- `window.open()` coordinates can target those screen coordinate spaces.
- `moveTo()` and `moveBy()` can place an eligible popup on another screen.
- `screenschange` and `currentscreenchange` report topology changes.
- `requestFullscreen({ screen })` can target a returned `ScreenDetailed`.

The OS must expose an **extended desktop**. Mirrored displays do not provide an independent workspace. Window managers, enterprise policy, VDI sessions, or kiosk policy may still clamp placement and sizing.

The current permission name is:

```js
await navigator.permissions.query({ name: "window-management" });
```

The old `window-placement` alias was removed in Chrome 125.

The API does **not** require PWA installation. A normal HTTPS page can use it with user permission. Installation merely gives the page an app-like window and OS launcher integration.

### Exact fallback

1. Test the API, not the user agent:

   ```js
   const canManageScreens = "getScreenDetails" in window;
   ```

2. Obtain permission during a dedicated setup action and catch `NotAllowedError`. Do not request permission and then depend on the original activation still being valid for a popup.

3. Cache the latest screen details and update them on `screenschange`.

4. On a later explicit “Open presentation” click, synchronously open the required popup using cached coordinates. Treat `null` as popup blocking.

5. If the API is absent or permission is denied:
   - Open one ordinary popup from the click.
   - Do not guess an off-screen coordinate.
   - Tell the user to drag it to the desired display.
   - Put a visible **Fullscreen** button inside that window.
   - Save application role/layout preferences, but let the user place the window again.

Ordinary `window.open()`, `moveTo()`, and `moveBy()` may be honored, clamped, or ignored by the browser/window manager. Firefox can honor some cross-screen coordinate requests, but because it cannot enumerate displays, that is not a reliable placement strategy.

## 2. Fullscreen across screens

### Ordinary fullscreen

Plain `element.requestFullscreen()` is broadly supported on desktop and Android. It normally fills the screen containing the relevant browser window, subject to the user agent and OS.

Important exceptions:

- iPad Safari has partial element-fullscreen support.
- iPhone Safari still does not expose general `Element.requestFullscreen()`.
- iOS WebView does not support it.
- Fullscreen requires a fully active document, an allowed `fullscreen` Permissions Policy, and normally transient user activation.
- Switching tabs/apps, navigating, or pressing Escape exits fullscreen.

For an embedded cross-origin document, delegate explicitly:

```html
<iframe src="…" allow="fullscreen"></iframe>
```

### Target-screen fullscreen

Only desktop Chromium implements:

```js
await element.requestFullscreen({ screen: targetScreenDetailed });
```

Firefox and Safari do not implement the `screen` option. Unsupported browsers may silently ignore unknown dictionary members and enter fullscreen on the current screen, so successful promise resolution does **not** prove that the requested monitor was selected.

### Multiple fullscreen displays

Chrome 104 added the fullscreen-companion behavior: one user activation can request fullscreen on one screen and open a companion popup on another.

Chrome 127 added the desktop-only `automatic-fullscreen` content setting, which can permit fullscreen without a fresh gesture and enables multiple-display fullscreen scenarios. It is blocked by default:

- Sites can query it but cannot trigger the permission prompt.
- Initial user-facing granting is restricted to security-sensitive applications such as Isolated Web Apps.
- Enterprise policy can grant additional origins.
- Installing an ordinary PWA does not grant it.

### Exact fallback

- If target-screen fullscreen is unavailable, first open or move the presentation window, ask the user to place it on the desired monitor, and expose a fullscreen button in that window.
- If ordinary fullscreen is unavailable, use a maximized/responsive standalone window and retain an obvious “presentation mode” that hides application controls.
- Never assume `display: "fullscreen"` in the PWA manifest selects a monitor. It only requests an installed-app display mode.
- Do not attempt simultaneous fullscreen calls in a loop unless `automatic-fullscreen` is already granted. Otherwise require separate user actions.

## 3. Presentation API

### Actual support and scope

`PresentationRequest` is implemented in Chromium browsers:

- Chrome desktop and Android from 47.
- Chromium Edge from 79.
- Chromium-derived Opera and Samsung Internet are recorded as mirrored implementations.
- Firefox and Safari do not implement it.
- Android WebView, iOS browsers, and iOS WebView do not implement it.

It requires HTTPS in current Chromium.

The API covers an implementation-dependent set of presentation displays, potentially including:

- Attached HDMI/DVI monitors.
- Miracast displays.
- Chromecast or compatible network receivers.
- Other browser-supported receiving user agents.

It does **not** return screen coordinates or let the site silently pick a named monitor. `start()` opens a browser-controlled permission/device chooser. Even where the interface exists, there may be no compatible display or transport.

`start()` must be called from transient user activation. It can reject because there are no displays, the user canceled, permission was denied, or the receiver could not be started.

### Exact fallback

```js
const canPresent = "PresentationRequest" in window;
```

If available:

1. Construct the request over HTTPS.
2. Use `getAvailability()` only to improve button state.
3. If availability monitoring rejects, keep the button enabled; discovery may still occur when `start()` runs.
4. Call `request.start()` directly from a user click.
5. Handle cancellation and no-display rejection as normal outcomes.

If unavailable:

- **Same-machine second monitor:** use Window Management when supported; otherwise use a popup plus manual drag and fullscreen.
- **Chromecast:** use the Google Cast Web Sender SDK, which is a separate vendor API.
- **AirPlay/media-only:** expose native media controls or the browser/platform’s AirPlay route.
- **Cross-browser arbitrary receiver:** open a receiver URL on the second device and pair it using a short code or QR code over WebSocket/WebRTC.
- **No scripted integration:** provide instructions for the browser or OS “Cast”, “Screen mirroring”, or “Use as separate display” UI.

A JavaScript polyfill cannot generally reproduce device discovery, OS routing, or trusted display selection.

## 4. Installed PWAs and multi-window placement

### Installation support

- Chrome and Edge install desktop PWAs on Windows, macOS, Linux, and ChromeOS.
- Safari supports Add to Dock website apps on macOS 14+.
- Firefox desktop requires a third-party extension rather than providing native PWA installation.
- Android Chromium can install a WebAPK or fall back to a shortcut.
- iOS/iPadOS support manually added home-screen web apps; all browser products use WebKit there.

Installation does not change the underlying engine’s API matrix. A Safari web app still has no Window Management, Presentation API, target-screen fullscreen, or `launch_handler`.

### `launch_handler`

Chromium 110+ supports:

```json
{
  "launch_handler": {
    "client_mode": ["navigate-new", "navigate-existing"]
  }
}
```

Semantics:

- `navigate-new`: create a new installed-app client/window where the platform supports it.
- `navigate-existing`: focus an existing client and navigate it.
- `focus-existing`: focus an existing client without navigation; deliver launch data through `launchQueue`.
- `auto`: browser/platform decides.

Desktop platforms can normally select `navigate-new`. Mobile platforms commonly support only one app client and route to an existing instance. The value can be an ordered list; the first supported value is chosen. If the browser does not support `launch_handler`, it ignores the member and uses its default app-launch behavior.

`launch_handler` controls **OS launch routing**, not:

- JavaScript popup permission.
- Which physical monitor receives the window.
- Window coordinates or size.
- Fullscreen permission.
- The number of windows that may remain

I read this as a 2026 compatibility verification - I cross-checked implementation data, vendor documentation, and current specifications, then mapped each unsupported path to a concrete fallback.

**Verified 2026-08-13.** “Supported” below means available without experimental flags; it does not imply that every OS, receiver protocol, or window manager will honor every request.

## Support matrix

| Capability | Chrome / Chromium Edge | Firefox | Safari / WebKit | Mobile |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Window Management API: `getScreenDetails()`, `ScreenDetails` | **Yes, desktop 100+** | No | No | Not exposed on Android, iOS, or WebView |
| Place `window.open()` on a selected screen | **Yes, desktop**, after Window Management permission | Legacy coordinates may cross screens, but no enumeration API or reliable topology | No reliable cross-screen API | No reliable support |
| `requestFullscreen()` on current screen | Yes | Yes | Yes on desktop; standard API since Safari 16.4 | Android yes; iPad partial; arbitrary element fullscreen unavailable on iPhone |
| `requestFullscreen({screen})` | **Yes, desktop 100+** | No | No | No |
| Presentation API | **Yes, Chromium 47+**, subject to available transport/receiver | No | No | Chromium Android yes; Android WebView no; Safari/iOS no |
| Installed desktop PWA | Chrome/Edge on Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS | No native desktop installation without an extension | macOS 14+ “Add to Dock” web apps | Android install varies between WebAPK/shortcut; iOS/iPadOS manual Add to Home Screen |
| `launch_handler.client_mode` | **Chromium 110+** | No | No | Exposed in Chromium, but mobile may enforce a single app client |
| Deterministic multiple PWA windows | Desktop Chromium can request `navigate-new` | No standard installed-PWA behavior | No `launch_handler`; user-controlled windows only | Must assume single-client behavior |
| Programmatically choose monitor for PWA launch | **No declarative manifest feature**; use Window Management after launch | No | No | No |

Opera and other desktop Chromium derivatives will generally inherit Chromium behavior, but they should be feature-tested rather than inferred from branding.

## 1. Window Management API

### Verified support

`window.getScreenDetails()` and the related screen enumeration/event interfaces are implemented in desktop Chromium from Chrome 100. MDN compatibility data reports:

- Chrome 100+
- Edge as Chromium mirror
- Firefox: unsupported
- Safari/iOS: unsupported
- Chrome Android: unsupported
- Android WebView: unsupported

Chrome Status independently records it as desktop-only and explicitly says the API was not initially exposed on mobile or WebView.

The API requires:

- HTTPS/secure context.
- The `window-management` permission.
- A permitting `Permissions-Policy` for embedded contexts.
- A user gesture for popup creation.
- Continued cooperation from the OS/window manager; coordinates remain requests, not authority.

Since Chrome 125, the old `window-placement` permission alias is removed. New code must query or declare **`window-management`**, not `window-placement`.

Installation is **not** required for screen enumeration or the base popup placement behavior. The newer proposed `maximize()`, `minimize()`, `restore()`, and `setResizable()` controls are different: as of this check they remain behind a Chrome 154 developer flag and their draft requires an installed web app. They are not production baseline.

### Exact fallback

Use screen-aware placement only when the API is present and permission succeeds:

```js
const supportsWindowManagement =
  typeof window.getScreenDetails === "function";

async function openOnScreen(url, screen) {
  return window.open(
    url,
    "_blank",
    `left=${screen.availLeft},top=${screen.availTop},` +
      `width=${screen.availWidth},height=${screen.availHeight}`
  );
}
```

If unsupported, permission is denied, or the popup is blocked:

1. Open an ordinary popup from the same user click:
   ```js
   const popup = window.open(url, "_blank");
   ```
2. Tell the user to drag it to the desired monitor.
3. Put an **Enter fullscreen** button inside that popup so fullscreen gets its own fresh user activation.
4. If `window.open()` returns `null`, navigate the current tab or expose a normal link with `target="_blank"`.

Legacy `screen`, `screenX`, `screenY`, `moveTo()`, and guessed `left`/`top` coordinates are only best-effort fallbacks. Firefox may permit cross-screen coordinates, but without topology enumeration the app cannot safely distinguish monitors, scaling, negative coordinates, or available work areas.

## 2. Presentation API

### Verified support

The API remains **limited availability and experimental**:

- Chromium 47+, including Chromium Android and Chromium Edge.
- No Firefox implementation.
- No Safari or iOS implementation.
- No Android WebView implementation.

API presence does not prove that a compatible display exists. The browser still needs an available transport and receiver capable of loading one of the requested presentation URLs. The specification permits attached HDMI/Miracast displays, Chromecast-like network displays, and both one-UA and two-UA rendering, but implementations do not have to support every mechanism.

`PresentationRequest.start()` must run from transient user activation. It can reject when:

- no compatible display is found,
- the user cancels or denies access,
- the context is sandboxed,
- the requested URL or transport is unsupported.

`getAvailability()` is optional in practical terms: even a supporting implementation may reject availability monitoring and defer discovery until `start()`.

### Exact fallback

```js
const supportsPresentation =
  typeof window.PresentationRequest === "function";

if (supportsPresentation) {
  const request = new PresentationRequest(["/receiver"]);

  try {
    const availability = await request.getAvailability();
    // Update UI from availability.value and its change event.
  } catch {
    // Keep the Present button in an "availability unknown" state.
    // Actual discovery will occur when start() is called.
  }

  presentButton.onclick = async () => {
    try {
      const connection = await request.start();
      // Attach message/state handlers.
    } catch {
      // User cancelled, denied access, or no receiver was found.
      showFallbackChoices();
    }
  };
}
```

Fallback by target type:

- **Locally attached monitor/projector:** use the Window Management popup flow. Without that API, open a popup and instruct the user to move it, then fullscreen it from a button in that window.
- **Generic second device:** show a receiver URL or QR code and synchronize controller/receiver through WebSocket or WebRTC. `BroadcastChannel` only works for same-origin contexts within the same browser storage partition and is not a cross-device fallback.
- **Media-only playback:** expose native `<video controls>` and the platform route picker. For product-specific casting, use the Google Cast Web Sender SDK or the applicable native AirPlay integration instead of pretending Presentation API is portable.
- **No popup/receiver:** present in the current tab.

## 3. Fullscreen across screens

### Ordinary fullscreen

Ordinary `Element.requestFullscreen()` is broadly supported on desktop Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari, and on Android browsers.

Important exceptions:

- iPadOS has partial arbitrary-element fullscreen support, including browser overlays and swipe-to-exit behavior.
- iPhone does not support arbitrary `Element.requestFullscreen()` according to current MDN compatibility data. Native video fullscreen is separate behavior.
- Fullscreen may be blocked by `Permissions-Policy: fullscreen`.
- It normally requires transient user activation.
- Changing tabs, navigating, or switching applications may exit fullscreen.

### Targeting a particular screen

`requestFullscreen({ screen: ScreenDetailed })` is desktop-Chromium-only from Chrome 100. Firefox and Safari do not implement the `screen` option. Chrome’s own documentation states that unsupported browsers silently ignore that option, so successful ordinary fullscreen does not prove the requested monitor was honored.

Use:

```js
async function fullscreenOn(element, targetScreen) {
  if (typeof window.getScreenDetails === "function" && targetScreen) {
    await element.requestFullscreen({ screen: targetScreen });
  } else if (document.fullscreenEnabled) {
    await element.requestFullscreen();
  } else {
    applyViewportFallback(element);
  }
}
```

A dictionary member cannot be reliably detected by checking `FullscreenOptions.prototype`. Gate cross-screen behavior on `getScreenDetails()`, permission success, and the selected `ScreenDetailed`; still treat placement as best effort.

### Multiple simultaneous fullscreen surfaces

Do not assume one click can make several windows fullscreen everywhere.

Desktop Chrome 127 added an **Automatic Fullscreen** site setting, but:

- it is blocked by default,
- websites cannot prompt for it,
- users must enable it in Chrome settings/site information, or an enterprise administrator must allow the origin,
- Chrome Status expects it to remain Chromium-only,
- mobile is not supported.

Chrome 104 does permit a useful narrower case: from one activation, a site can fullscreen on one screen and open a companion popup on another screen. That does not make every companion fullscreen.

Exact baseline fallback:

1. Make only the primary presentation fullscreen.
2. Keep notes/tool windows ordinary and positioned where supported.
3. Put an explicit fullscreen button in each companion window.
4. On unsupported browsers, have the user move each window before pressing its fullscreen button.
5. On iPhone or when fullscreen is unavailable, use a viewport presentation mode:

```css
.viewport-presentation {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 0;
  width: 100vw;
  height: 100dvh;
  z-index: 2147483647;
  background: black;
}
```

This hides page content but cannot hide browser/OS chrome.

## 4. Installed PWAs and multi-window behavior

### Installation by OS/browser

- **Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS:** Chrome and Edge install PWAs into standalone application windows.
- **Firefox desktop:** no native PWA installation; an extension is required.
- **macOS 14+:** Safari supports Add to Dock web apps, but not Chromium’s Window Management or Launch Handler APIs.
- **iOS/iPadOS:** manual Add to Home Screen. Standalone is the only supported app display mode. `fullscreen` falls back to `standalone`; `minimal-ui` may fall back to a browser shortcut. Separate installations have isolated storage.
- **Android:** the result may be a WebAPK, shortcut, or vendor-specific package. A shortcut is not equivalent to an installed app and cannot use capabilities requiring installation.

Installed status does not transform unsupported Web APIs into supported ones. A Safari web app still lacks `getScreenDetails()` and `launch_handler`; an installed Chromium PWA still needs Window Management permission.

### Multiple PWA windows

Chromium 110+ supports:

```json
{
  "display": "standalone",
  "display_override": [
    "window-controls-overlay",
    "standalone"
  ],
  "launch_handler": {
    "client_mode": ["navigate-new", "auto"]
  }
}
```

Semantics:

- `navigate-new`: create a new web-app client where the platform supports it.
- `navigate-existing`: focus and navigate an existing client; if none exists, create one.
- `focus-existing`: focus an existing client without navigation and deliver the target through `launchQueue`; if none exists, create one.
- `auto`: browser/platform decides. Desktop commonly chooses a new window; mobile commonly reuses one.
- An array selects the first value supported by the browser/platform.
- If `launch_handler` itself is unsupported, it is ignored and the browser’s default launch behavior applies.

`navigate-new` controls client routing, **not monitor selection, coordinates, window size, or fullscreen**. For deterministic monitor placement, the launched app must subsequently use Window Management and open/place another context from a user gesture.

Do not use `ServiceWorker.clients.openWindow()` as a placement fallback: it cannot select a monitor, request coordinates, or guarantee a standalone PWA window.

For unsupported browsers/platforms, the exact fallback is:

- Default to a single application client.
- Implement documents/views as in-app panels or app-managed tabs.
- Offer a user-triggered **Open in new window** action using `window.open()`.
- Preserve state through URL parameters plus IndexedDB/server storage.
- Let the user arrange the resulting windows manually.

The experimental `display_override: "tabbed"` mode is not a general multi-window solution. Chrome documentation only demonstrates completed launch support on ChromeOS, and unsupported browsers follow the manifest fallback chain.

## Evidence groups

### Group A: primary specifications and vendor implementation records

- [W3C Window Management Working Draft](https://www.w3.org/TR/window-management/)
- [Chrome: Window Management API](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/capabilities/web-apis/window-management)
- [Chrome Status: Window Management](https://chromestatus.com/feature/5252960583942144)
- [Chrome Status: Fullscreen Companion Window](https://chromestatus.com/feature/5173162437246976)
- [Chrome Status: Automatic Fullscreen](https
